What's missing from the map of global internet infrastructure?

Stephen Song

Tim Kelly

November 20, 2026

This page in:

English

English

The Open Fiber Data Standard provides a common framework for mapping terrestrial fiber networks and improving visibility into global internet infrastructure. Pictured, a close up of empty conduits for fiber optic cables in a construction site in Brake, Germany. / Image: Heide Pinkall / Shutterstock.com

Optic fiber cables form the backbone of global communications. An often-cited statistic is that submarine cables carry approximately 99% of the world's Internet traffic. Unfortunately, the typical framing of that statistic contains a subtle error. It is true that approximately 99% of internet traffic is carried by undersea cables, but this refers to 99% of intercontinental traffic. In a well-functioning internet, the majority of traffic for a typical user is not likely to travel via undersea fibre optic cables but remain on national terrestrial networks.
To know where these are, the World Bank Group has supported the development of the Open Fiber Data Standard (OFDS), a common language for describing and mapping terrestrial fibre optic networks. Since 2022, the work has been guided by a consortium of organizations, including the World Bank Group, the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), the Internet Society, Mozilla, Liquid Intelligent Technologies, CSquared, and Digital Council Africa. Since that time, the importance of global internet resiliency has risen dramatically in the wake of multiple disruptions to fibre optic cables, most recently affecting air traffic control in the US. OFDS is more important than ever as a result.
When we connect to the internet, our interactions are often localized because we are communicating with people or services in our own countries or region. When we access international services and content, we are often served by local Content Distribution Networks (CDNs). The globally distributed nature of a CDN means reduced distance between users and website resources. Instead of connecting to a website’s origin server, a CDN lets users connect to a geographically closer data center. Less travel time means faster service. It is true that CDNs must be refreshed from their global sources, but their very existence suggests that local traffic predominates.
Our growing social and economic dependence on internet infrastructure, combined with some serious cable breaks in the Red Sea, off the coast of Côte d’Ivoire, and elsewhere in recent years, has focused more attention on the need for a more resilient global internet infrastructure. Much-needed effort is now being placed on critical submarine cable issues such as route diversity and the availability of repair ships. However, if we accept that terrestrial fibre optic infrastructure plays an equally important role in internet infrastructure resilience as submarine cable infrastructure, we should ask why terrestrial fibre has not received the same level of attention. The answer may lie in the image below.
Telegeography, a telecommunications data and research firm, maintains an excellent resource in its submarine cable map, tracking the development and lifespan of more than 600 undersea cables. Resources like this provide wonderful visibility for submarine cable infrastructure. However, the absence of similar data on terrestrial fibre optic infrastructure perpetuates the idea that terrestrial fibre is of lesser importance. The very lack of visibility of terrestrial infrastructure in these maps diminishes its significance.

What’s missing from this picture? / Credit: Telegeography

 
Yet terrestrial fibre infrastructure plays a critical role not only in regional connectivity but also in undersea cable resilience. When undersea cables were disrupted in the Baltic Sea, restoration of internet services was enabled in part by routing traffic through terrestrial links. Terrestrial and undersea cable infrastructure are two sides of the coin of global internet resilience. One must wonder whether the lack of visibility of terrestrial fibre optic infrastructure has led to it largely being left out of global discussions on internet infrastructure resilience.
But it is not just for resilience that terrestrial fibre networks matter.  Terrestrial fibre networks are critical to the mission of connecting the unconnected because of their sheer capacity.  Terrestrial fibre networks can carry orders of magnitude more data than any other access technology.  This means they can support multiple operators and purposes. They also represent a long-term investment in infrastructure.  Terrestrial fibre networks can last more than 20 years and often may be upgraded in place. As such, terrestrial fibre networks are the solid foundation on which long-term, affordable, resilient internet infrastructure is built.
This is what makes OFDS such an important initiative now. The common descriptive framework enabled by OFDS makes it possible to assemble the jigsaw puzzle of connectivity infrastructure in a collaborative and distributed manner. It also enables different levels of sharing, ranging from essential public information to more sensitive data restricted to regulators or operators themselves.
The multi-stakeholder nature of OFDS means that regulators, operators, researchers, infrastructure investors, and civil society can all have a voice in what should be captured by the data standard. Since 2025, the Internet Society has hosted the secretariat and provided support to the independent governance board convened for the first time in August of this year.
Anyone interested in the overall resilience of global Internet infrastructure should be interested in developing a clearer picture of the deployment and interconnection of national, regional, and international terrestrial fibre optic networks. OFDS is the beginning of that conversation. To find out more, visit OFDS’ website or get in touch at outreach@ofds.info.
